title: Olivia Wilde's 'The Invite' Crashes the Indie Box Office with a $56K Per-Screen Average
summary: In the world of indie cinema, a platform release is a delicate dance: open in a handful of theaters, generate word-of-mouth, and hope the per-screen average is high enough to justify expansion. Olivia Wilde's "The Invite" just executed a near-perfect pirouette. The film, which A24 acquired in an aggressive bidding war at Sundance, opened on seven screens and grossed $393,357. That's an average of $56,194 per theater—a figure that puts it in elite company. To put that in perspective, last week John Early's "Maddie's Secret" grossed $58,206 from a single screen. "The Invite" nearly matched that average across seven times as many locations. It's a testament to Wilde's drawing power and the film's critical momentum. A24 has a storied history with platform releases, though it's increasingly shifted to wide openings. Still, "The Invite" is already outpacing some recent favorites. It nearly matched the opening weekend of "The Moment" starring Charli XCX, which made $427K but from just four theaters, giving it an average almost double. "The Invite" is also well ahead of "Mother Mary," which averaged a meager $33K from five screens and faded after five weeks. The high-water mark for A24 remains "Marty Supreme," which from six screens brought in $863K on opening weekend—a staggering $144K per screen. "The Invite" isn't in that stratosphere, but its numbers suggest a healthy run. For context, "Pillion," another A24 title, opened on four screens with a $60K average and eventually expanded to 369 screens, finishing with a strong $3.8 million. Elsewhere on the specialized chart, holdovers "Maddie's Secret" and "Rose of Nevada" each added eight screens in their second weekends and are still performing well. New entries include Carla Simón's Cannes drama "Romeria," which landed at #6 with $15,193, and the Italian drama "For the Love of a Woman" at #8 with $4,294. In a heartwarming twist, Janus Films' "Blue Heron" crept back into the top 10 in its 11th weekend, approaching $600K domestically. IndieWire also exclusively announced its streaming date on The Criterion Channel. For now, all eyes are on "The Invite." If it follows the trajectory of past A24 successes, it won't be an exclusive party for long.
why_it_matters: High per-screen averages at indie theaters show that audiences want stories outside the superhero blockbuster mold—if 'The Invite' succeeds, more risk-taking films might get funded and find their way to your local cinema.

background_read: Sundance Film Festival (held annually in Utah, USA) is the most important marketplace for independent films—many small movies are discovered and bought there by distributors like A24 (an independent entertainment company known for bold, artistic films).
A platform release is a classic indie strategy: a film opens in just a few cities and relies on reviews and word-of-mouth to build demand before expanding to more theaters.
Olivia Wilde, besides acting, has directed acclaimed features, and her name alone can draw audiences to a movie.
Per-screen averages are watched closely because a high number means the film was 'sold out' in those few locations, signaling a healthy appetite for a wider release.

perspectives.perspective: Positive – a sign of a strong indie market
perspectives.description: A $56K average signals genuine audience excitement, not just industry hype. If the film expands successfully, it can prove that character-driven stories still have a place in a market dominated by big franchises.

perspectives.perspective: Negative – per-screen averages can be misleading
perspectives.description: Small numbers of screens in major cities can inflate averages—once a film goes wide, the numbers often drop fast. A hot opening weekend in New York and LA may not translate to sustained interest in suburban multiplexes.

Platform releases are a high-stakes game: go too slowly and momentum dies; expand too fast and you burn out. Studios study past trajectories, but word-of-mouth is unpredictable. The history of A24 shows that even with a strong start, not every film becomes a 'Marty Supreme.'

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking – what expansion could mean for diversity in theaters
perspectives.description: If 'The Invite' follows 'Pillion's path to 369 screens and a $3.8 million final gross, it could encourage more distributors to acquire female-directed, unconventional narratives. Success here might greenlight films that reflect more varied lived experiences on American screens.
